title: Trump’s Pacific Islands Blind Spot
gist: Derek Grossman argues the second Trump administration has abandoned the Pacific islands—16 nations and territories with zero Senate-confirmed U.S. ambassadors more than 18 months in—while Beijing sustains diplomatic cadence and expands strategic agreements with the Cook Islands and Solomon Islands. He ties the neglect to a broader strategic narrowing from 'Indo-Pacific' back to 'Asia-Pacific' and warns it undermines the second island chain (Japan to Palau) that a prolonged war with China would depend on.

insights.claim: More than 18 months into the second Trump administration, the United States has zero Senate-confirmed ambassadors to any of the 16 Pacific island nations and territories.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: A measurable, trackable indicator of U.S. diplomatic bandwidth in Oceania—ambassadorial confirmations are the cheapest leading signal of whether Washington intends to contest Chinese influence there.

insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: The bar for 'engagement' has fallen to a deputy-secretary visit, signaling how little political capital Washington is spending in a region China courts at foreign-minister level.

insights.claim: The only new regional initiative the second Trump administration has announced for the Pacific islands is a deep-sea mining collaboration with the Cook Islands on critical minerals.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: Deep-sea mining is the single Pacific policy line with commercial exposure—watch Cook Islands seabed licensing as the one place U.S. Pacific policy translates into a tradable resource story.

insights.claim: The first Trump administration actively prioritized the Pacific islands—sending sitting secretaries of state and defense to Micronesia and Palau for the first time and hosting a White House summit with all three Freely Associated States leaders—making the second term's neglect a reversal of Trump's own precedent rather than a continuation of it.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: Undercuts the assumption that Pacific neglect is ideological; it is discretionary and therefore reversible on short notice if attention shifts.

insights.claim: The Biden administration built a durable Pacific architecture—renewed Compacts of Free Association with the Freely Associated States, a Papua New Guinea coast guard security deal, reopening the Solomon Islands embassy after nearly three decades, new embassies in Tonga and Vanuatu, and the first standalone 'Pacific Partnerships Strategy' national security document.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: The Compacts give Washington security dominance over a large swath of the Pacific regardless of diplomatic drift—an installed base that limits how much ground China can actually take.

themes.theme: Energy crisis and tourism shock in import-dependent island economies

insights.claim: The war against Iran has caused a global energy crisis that disproportionately harms Pacific island states because of their near-total dependence on imported fuel and goods, with cost increases compounding as suppliers like Australia and Singapore pass on their own steeper costs.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: Small import-dependent economies are the highest-beta victims of an oil shock; watch for sovereign distress, fuel subsidy blowouts, and IMF/China lending demand across Oceania.

insights.claim: Tourism—described as the economic lifeblood of Pacific island nations—is in serious jeopardy as consumers cut intercontinental travel to save money during the energy crisis.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: Long-haul discretionary travel is the transmission channel from an oil shock to Pacific GDP; airline capacity cuts on trans-Pacific routes are the early tell.

insights.claim: The effective elimination of USAID has damaged Pacific island states across climate adaptation, disaster preparedness, public health, fisheries management, and humanitarian assistance simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: Withdrawn U.S. development funding leaves a service gap that Beijing can fill cheaply—aid vacuums historically convert into security agreements.

insights.claim: Trump's denial of climate change is the single most destructive U.S. policy for standing in the Pacific islands because the entire region treats climate as an existential issue, and unlike in his first term there is no offsetting positive engagement for islanders to look past it.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: Climate framing is the price of admission in Oceania diplomacy; U.S. absence there is a structural, not cyclical, advantage for China.

insights.claim: Beijing's Pacific playbook is cadence rather than breakthroughs—convening Pacific island foreign ministers, expanding strategic agreements with the Cook Islands and Solomon Islands, and maintaining steady senior diplomatic engagement—so perception of consistency accrues to China even where individual initiatives produce nothing.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: Influence in small states is bought with attention frequency, not deal size—a low-cost strategy the U.S. cannot counter with episodic high-level visits.

insights.claim: When China test-fired a ballistic missile that landed in the South Pacific in July 2026, the U.S. State Department condemned the test but reaffirmed defense commitments only generically to 'allies and partners' without naming Pacific island countries, treating it as a long-term arms control issue rather than a regional threat.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: A live demonstration that Chinese strike range now reaches beyond the second island chain, met with a U.S. response that signals ambiguity about extended deterrence in Oceania.

themes.theme: From Indo-Pacific to Asia-Pacific: a narrowing U.S. strategic aperture

insights.claim: The White House is quietly retiring the 'Indo-Pacific' framing—which included India and the Indian Ocean—in favor of a narrower 'Asia-Pacific' concept focused on East Asian deterrence against China, evidenced by Hegseth's Shangri-La Dialogue speech avoiding the term and Trump renaming Indo-Pacific Command back to Pacific Command.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: A formal downgrade of India's role in U.S. Asia strategy—bearish for U.S.-India defense-industrial tie-ups and bullish for concentration of U.S. posture spending in Japan, Korea, and the Philippines.

insights.claim: Secretary of State Marco Rubio's meeting with the 'Squad'—Australia, Japan, the Philippines, and the United States, swapping the Philippines in for India relative to the Quad—signals that first island chain defense has displaced the broader Quad architecture as Washington's operational priority.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: Watch Philippine basing, munitions, and coast guard procurement as the beneficiary of the Quad-to-Squad shift; India-linked defense cooperation is the funding loser.

insights.claim: Hegseth has repeatedly labeled Japan, South Korea, and the Philippines 'model allies' specifically for pledging a higher share of GDP to defense, making burden-sharing percentages the explicit currency of favored-ally status in the second Trump administration.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: Defense-budget-to-GDP announcements from Asian allies are now a direct lever on U.S. treatment—supportive for Japanese and Korean defense contractors.

themes.theme: Second island chain as war-fighting infrastructure

insights.claim: The narrowing of U.S. focus to the Taiwan Strait, East China Sea, and South China Sea paradoxically raises the importance of the second island chain—stretching from Japan to Palau—because U.S. territories (Guam, American Samoa, the Northern Mariana Islands) and the Freely Associated States would host the deployments supporting any fight closer to China.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: Second-island-chain basing, airfield, and port hardening is where Pacific defense capex logically concentrates even as diplomacy is defunded.
insights.locator: All of this adds up to a United States that is more worried

insights.claim: Improving range and lethality of Chinese weapons makes distributed basing across many Pacific island territories a military necessity rather than a preference, because concentrating U.S. troops and resources in any single location is now untenable.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: Distributed posture means access agreements with many small states become a hard military requirement—each lost diplomatic relationship removes an option from the war plan.

insights.claim: Judged even by the Trump administration's own metric of competing militarily with China, neglecting diplomacy and development in the Pacific is counterproductive because deterrence depends on being seen as a credible and reliable partner, not only on military prowess.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: The core argument: hard-power-only strategy degrades the access rights that hard power requires—a self-defeating loop worth tracking through base access renegotiations.
insights.quote: Deterrence is built not only with military prowess but also with sustained diplomacy and trusted political relationships.

insights.claim: Better U.S. relations with Pacific island nations function as a preemptive block on Beijing expanding its own security partnerships across the region, making diplomacy a denial strategy rather than merely goodwill.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: Each new China-Pacific security pact should be read as a direct subtraction from U.S. wartime access, not as a symbolic win.
